set_title: Fever, emboli or a mitral rumble: tumor, vegetation or rheumatic valve
stem: A 6-month-old girl has infantile spasms and hypopigmented patches on the trunk. Echocardiography shows multiple well-circumscribed masses in the ventricular walls. There is no fever and blood cultures are sterile.
oneliner: 6-month-old girl + infantile spasms + hypopigmented patches + multiple ventricular wall masses → ?
ask: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.B: Myxoma is a **solitary atrial tumor in adults**
whyNot.A: Endocarditis needs **fever and positive cultures**; she has neither
whyNot.D: Rheumatic fever follows **strep pharyngitis in school-age children**
whyNot.E: Mitral stenosis is an **adult sequela** with a murmur, not ventricular masses

why: Tuberous sclerosis (TSC1 or TSC2) causes seizures, ash-leaf spots and **ventricular rhabdomyomas**, the most common fetal and infant cardiac tumor, which often regress spontaneously.

Adults 40-60, women more often; left atrium
Diastolic rumble and **tumor plop that change with position**

**Gelatinous mass with stellate cells in myxoid stroma**
Infective endocarditis
Damaged valve, IV drug use, prosthetic valve, dental procedure
New regurgitant murmur
Fever, Roth spots, splinter hemorrhages, Janeway lesions
**Vegetations; positive blood cultures**
Rheumatic mitral stenosis
Adults years after rheumatic fever
**Opening snap then diastolic rumble** at the apex
Left atrial enlargement, atrial fibrillation
**Fibrotic, fused commissures with thick chordae**
Cardiac rhabdomyoma
Infants and children with tuberous sclerosis
Often silent; may obstruct outflow
Seizures, ash-leaf spots, TSC1 or TSC2 mutation
**Hamartoma with large vacuolated glycogen-rich cells (spider cells)**
Acute rheumatic fever
Children 5-15, 2-3 weeks after group A strep pharyngitis
New regurgitant murmur (mitral)
**Migratory polyarthritis, carditis, chorea, erythema marginatum, nodules**
**Aschoff bodies with Anitschkow cells**; raised ASO, cultures negative

idea.rule: Infant + seizures + skin patches + ventricular masses = rhabdomyoma.

stem: A 24-year-old man has an LDL cholesterol of 280 mg/dL and a triglyceride level of 120 mg/dL. His father had a myocardial infarction at age 45.
oneliner: 24M + LDL 280 + triglycerides 120 + father with MI at 45 → ?
ask: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: Combined hyperlipidemia also **raises triglycerides**; his triglycerides are normal at 120 mg/dL
whyNot.B: Lipoprotein lipase deficiency gives **triglycerides above 1,000 mg/dL** in childhood; his are 120
whyNot.C: Hypertriglyceridemia has **raised triglycerides with normal LDL**; he has the reverse
whyNot.D: Dysbetalipoproteinemia raises **both cholesterol and triglycerides**; his triglycerides are normal

why: A defective LDL receptor leaves LDL in the blood, so LDL is very high from birth while **triglycerides stay normal**, and coronary disease comes early. Statins still work in heterozygotes because they increase LDL receptors made from the normal allele.

head: LDL
Triglycerides
Exam and family clue
First-line drug
rows: Familial hypercholesterolemia
**Very high (190 mg/dL or more; above 500 in homozygotes)**
Normal
Tendon xanthomas, corneal arcus; autosomal dominant LDL receptor defect; early coronary disease
High-intensity statin; add ezetimibe or a PCSK9 inhibitor
Familial combined hyperlipidemia
Raised, or normal in some relatives
**Raised, with the pattern varying between relatives**
Early coronary disease; apoB overproduction; no tendon xanthomas
Statin; add a fibrate or omega-3 if triglycerides remain high
Hypertriglyceridemia
Normal or low
**Markedly raised (500 mg/dL or more)**
Pancreatitis risk, eruptive xanthomas; excess VLDL production
Fibrate (with lifestyle change and alcohol and sugar restriction)

idea.rule: Very high LDL with normal triglycerides and early coronary disease in the family = familial hypercholesterolemia.
also: Autosomal dominant LDL receptor defect; tendon xanthomas and corneal arcus are typical
Statins upregulate LDL receptors, so they work in heterozygotes

stem: A 40-year-old man has no symptoms. Fasting glucose is normal and BMI is 27 kg/m2. A fasting lipid panel is abnormal. Familial hypercholesterolemia and isolated hypertriglyceridemia are both being considered.
oneliner: 40M + asymptomatic + normal glucose + BMI 27 + abnormal lipid panel → FH or isolated hypertriglyceridemia?
ask: Which single finding favours familial hypercholesterolemia over isolated hypertriglyceridemia?

options.E: No symptoms at the time of testing

whyNot.A: A **normal glucose** is expected in both
whyNot.B: A **BMI of 27** is common to both
whyNot.E: Both are usually **silent until a complication**

why: Cholesterol-rich LDL deposits in tendons, so **Achilles tendon xanthomas** point to familial hypercholesterolemia. In isolated hypertriglyceridemia LDL is normal and the skin findings, when present, are eruptive xanthomas.

set_title: Kidney or ureter formed wrong: fused, missing or blocked
stem: A 29-year-old primigravid woman has ultrasonography at 20 weeks that shows no right kidney. The sonographer cannot yet tell whether the left kidney is also absent.
oneliner: 29F + 20 weeks + no right kidney seen + left kidney unclear → ?
ask: Which single finding on the same scan would favor bilateral renal agenesis over unilateral renal agenesis?

options.A: An amniotic fluid index of 2 cm
options.E: No ectopic kidney in the pelvis

whyNot.B: The right kidney is already absent in both conditions, so an **absent right ureter** fits either one
whyNot.C: The spine forms independently of the metanephros, so a **normal spine** fits either condition
whyNot.D: The heart is normal in both; it says nothing about whether the **left kidney** is present
whyNot.E: A pelvic search for the missing **right kidney** is negative in both conditions, so it does not separate them

answer: An amniotic fluid index of 2 cm
why: With one working kidney the fetus still makes urine and amniotic fluid stays normal. If both kidneys are absent there is no fetal urine, so severe oligohydramnios develops; the fetus lacks the fluid it needs for lung growth and has Potter facies and limb deformities. **Severe oligohydramnios means both kidneys are missing.**

head: Embryologic error
One side or both
Amniotic fluid and lungs
Imaging or exam clue
rows: Ureteropelvic junction obstruction
Incomplete recanalization of the proximal ureter narrows the junction with the renal pelvis
Usually one side (left more often than right); boys more than girls
Amniotic fluid and lungs normal when one kidney is affected
**Dilated renal pelvis and calyces with a normal-caliber ureter and a normal bladder**
Posterior urethral valves
Abnormal mucosal folds in the prostatic urethra block urine outflow (boys only)
Both sides: dilated ureters and kidneys on each side
Severe cases: oligohydramnios and pulmonary hypoplasia
**Distended, thick-walled bladder with dilated ureters and calyces on both sides**; dilated posterior urethra on voiding cystourethrography
Horseshoe kidney
Lower poles of the two kidneys fuse; ascent stops at the inferior mesenteric artery
Both kidneys, joined across the midline by an isthmus
Amniotic fluid and lungs normal
**Lower poles joined in front of the aorta, below the inferior mesenteric artery, with multiple renal arteries**; associated with Turner syndrome
Unilateral renal agenesis
Ureteric bud fails to form or to induce the metanephros on one side
One side
Amniotic fluid and lungs normal (the other kidney makes urine)
**One kidney absent and the other larger than normal (compensatory hypertrophy)**; creatinine usually normal
Bilateral renal agenesis (Potter sequence)
Same failure of ureteric bud induction, on both sides
Both sides
**Severe oligohydramnios (no fetal urine) with pulmonary hypoplasia, flat face and limb deformities; fatal**
Both kidneys and ureters absent; bladder small or not seen
Duplex collecting system
Early splitting of the ureteric bud (partial) or a second ureteric bud (complete)
Either side or both
Amniotic fluid and lungs normal

**Two renal pelves or ureters from one kidney**; the upper-pole ureter inserts lower and more medially (Weigert-Meyer rule) and is obstructed or ends in a ureterocele, while the lower-pole ureter refluxes

idea.rule: Severe oligohydramnios with pulmonary hypoplasia = both kidneys absent; normal fluid with a large solitary kidney = one absent.
also: Potter sequence: flat face, limb deformities, pulmonary hypoplasia
Death is from pulmonary hypoplasia, not from kidney failure
Both conditions share the failure of ureteric bud induction

set_title: Normal-gap acidosis from the kidney tubule: which defect
stem: A 20-month-old boy is brought for poor growth, frequent wet diapers and bowed legs. Slit-lamp examination shows crystals in the cornea. Serum studies show hypokalemia, hypophosphatemia and a normal anion gap metabolic acidosis, and urinalysis shows glucose and amino acids despite a normal serum glucose.
oneliner: 20-mo M + poor growth + wet diapers + bowed legs + corneal crystals + low K and phosphate + normal-gap acidosis + glucosuria and aminoaciduria → ?
ask: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: Distal RTA does not spill glucose and amino acids and does not explain his **corneal crystals**
whyNot.B: Isolated proximal RTA loses only bicarbonate; he also loses **glucose, amino acids and phosphate** and has **corneal crystals**
whyNot.C: Nephrogenic diabetes insipidus gives dilute polyuria without acidosis or glucosuria; he has a **normal anion gap acidosis with corneal crystals**
whyNot.E: Type 4 RTA raises potassium; his potassium is **low**

why: Cystine accumulates in lysosomes because the transporter cystinosin is defective. It crystallizes in the cornea and damages the proximal tubule, producing the Fanconi pattern of glucose, amino acid, phosphate and bicarbonate loss, with rickets. **Corneal crystals plus the Fanconi pattern in a young child = cystinosis.**

head: Defect and site
Serum potassium
Urine pH during acidosis
Other urine losses and complications
rows: Distal renal tubular acidosis (type 1)
Alpha-intercalated cells of the collecting duct cannot secrete H+ (H+-ATPase defect, amphotericin B, autoimmune disease)
Low
**Above 5.5 despite systemic acidosis**
Hypercalciuria and low urinary citrate: calcium phosphate stones and nephrocalcinosis; rickets or osteomalacia; no glucose or amino acids in the urine
Proximal renal tubular acidosis (type 2)
Proximal tubule reabsorbs too little HCO3- (carbonic anhydrase inhibition; the isolated form is rare)
Low
**Below 5.5 once serum bicarbonate has fallen to the lowered threshold**; alkaline if bicarbonate is infused
Bicarbonate wasting; rickets or osteomalacia; no stones; no glucose or amino acids unless Fanconi syndrome is also present
Hyperkalemic renal tubular acidosis (type 4)
Low aldosterone or aldosterone resistance in the collecting duct lowers K+ and H+ secretion and ammonium excretion
**High**
Below 5.5 (acidic)
Diabetic nephropathy (hyporeninemic hypoaldosteronism), ACE inhibitors, ARBs, spironolactone, trimethoprim, heparin
Fanconi syndrome
Generalized failure of proximal tubule reabsorption
Low
Below 5.5 once serum bicarbonate is low (proximal pattern)
**Glucosuria with a normal serum glucose, phosphaturia, aminoaciduria and bicarbonaturia**; hypophosphatemic rickets or osteomalacia, polyuria
Cystinosis
Autosomal recessive defect of the lysosomal cystine transporter (cystinosin, CTNS) damages the proximal tubule
Low
Below 5.5 (Fanconi pattern)
**Corneal cystine crystals on slit-lamp examination**; photophobia, failure to thrive, rickets, kidney failure in childhood

idea.rule: Corneal crystals with proximal tubule wasting in a toddler = cystinosis.
also: Autosomal recessive; CTNS gene encodes the lysosomal cystine transporter
Progresses to kidney failure in childhood

set_title: Cystic kidneys: which inherited or developmental disease
stem: A 26-year-old man has had two episodes of gross hematuria and has hypertension. CT shows multiple cysts in both kidneys.
oneliner: 26M + two episodes of gross hematuria + hypertension + multiple cysts in both kidneys → ?
ask: Which single additional finding would favor tuberous sclerosis complex over autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease?

whyNot.B: Hepatic cysts point toward **autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease**, not tuberous sclerosis
whyNot.C: Berry aneurysms accompany **autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease**, not tuberous sclerosis
whyNot.D: Flank pain with **hematuria** occurs in both conditions
whyNot.E: Both conditions are dominant, so inheritance does not separate them in a patient with **bilateral renal cysts**

why: Tuberous sclerosis (TSC1 or TSC2, which normally restrain mTOR) causes angiomyolipomas, hamartomas of fat, vessels and smooth muscle, that bleed and cause hematuria, alongside renal cysts. Autosomal dominant polycystic disease produces cysts without fat-containing masses. **A fat-containing renal mass means tuberous sclerosis.**

head: Age at presentation
Inheritance and gene
Kidney size and cyst pattern
Outside the kidney
rows: Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease
Adults, usually in their 30s to 40s
Autosomal dominant; PKD1 (polycystin-1, chromosome 16) in most, PKD2 (chromosome 4) in the rest
**Both kidneys enlarged, cysts in cortex and medulla**
Berry aneurysms, hepatic cysts, mitral valve prolapse; hypertension, hematuria and flank pain
Autosomal recessive polycystic kidney disease
Perinatal period or infancy
Autosomal recessive; PKHD1 (fibrocystin)
Both kidneys enlarged, with radially arranged elongated collecting-duct cysts
**Congenital hepatic fibrosis with portal hypertension**; Potter sequence with pulmonary hypoplasia in severe cases
Tuberous sclerosis complex
Infancy and childhood
Autosomal dominant; TSC1 (hamartin) or TSC2 (tuberin), which normally restrain mTOR
Multiple bilateral cysts and **fat-containing angiomyolipomas**
Seizures, ash-leaf macules, facial angiofibromas, shagreen patch, cortical tubers, cardiac rhabdomyomas
Multicystic dysplastic kidney
Prenatal period or infancy
Sporadic; not inherited
**One kidney replaced by non-communicating cysts of varying size with no functioning tissue**; the other kidney is normal (bilateral disease is fatal)
Atretic ureter on the affected side; usually no other organ involved
Medullary cystic kidney disease (nephronophthisis)
Nephronophthisis in childhood and adolescence; medullary cystic kidney disease in adults
Nephronophthisis autosomal recessive (nephrocystin, NPHP genes); medullary cystic kidney disease autosomal dominant (UMOD, MUC1)
**Small kidneys with cysts at the corticomedullary junction**
Chronic tubulointerstitial disease: polyuria, anemia, progressive kidney failure; retinitis pigmentosa in some nephronophthisis

idea.rule: Renal cysts plus fat-containing angiomyolipomas = tuberous sclerosis; cysts plus berry aneurysms and liver cysts = autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease.
also: Seizures, ash-leaf macules and cortical tubers accompany it
Angiomyolipomas can bleed; mTOR inhibitors shrink them
